title: Film Noir
description: Film noir lighting is a low-key, high-contrast setup: a hard key, often cut by a venetian gobo or a streetlamp cookie, leaves one cheek in true black while wet pavement returns silver. The camera sits at eye height on a 35mm or 50mm spherical lens, tungsten practicals as motivated sources, and blocking that isolates a figure in a doorway, an alley, or a pool of light.

sections.title: Narrative function

blocks.text: The shot withholds the room. A face is half a mask.
Guilt has to live in the sliver that remains, which is why voice-over can sit on this image without explaining the picture. Streets are wet so the night has a specular path back to the lens.
It is the wrong tool when the crime is colorful, fashionable, or futuristic. If the threat is a gelled primary, use Giallo.
If the night is neon and the year is now, use Neo-Noir. If the architecture itself is bent, use German Expressionism, not a wet street.

sections.title: How it works

blocks.text: Key with a hard Fresnel or open-face through slats, 45 to 90 degrees off camera, fill killed so the ratio sits near 8:1. Wet-down the street so the same key returns as bounce.
Practicals (desk lamp, cafe sign, streetlamp) must match the direction even if they are not the exposure. Lens: 35mm for a street, 50mm for a face, moderate stop so walls fall off.
Camera locked or a short dolly, eye level or a touch below. Prompt the gobo, the unfilled cheek, the wet asphalt, and 1940s crime blocking.

sections.title: When to use it

blocks.text: Use it when a character steps under a streetlamp and the shadow has to accuse them. Do not use it as a generic dark-crime grade on a color-saturated fashion interior.

sections.title: Compared with similar shots

blocks.text: Film noir is silver, hard, and unfilled. Neo-noir keeps the guilty geometry but paints it with color practicals.
Tech noir adds future screens as keys. Giallo is the opposite palette: hyper-saturated primaries, not black-and-white pools.
German Expressionism distorts the set; noir usually keeps real streets and lets light do the distortion. Kit cousins: Low-Key Lighting, Gobo Lighting, Wet-Down, Chiaroscuro.

sections.title: In film

blocks.text: The Third Man (wet Vienna, hard raking keys, a face in a doorway). Double Indemnity (venetian gobos, a confession in a dark living room).
The Big Combo (a fogged spotlight as the only map of a killing ground). Grammar, not frames to copy.

sections.title: What usually goes wrong

blocks.text: The usual wrong cousin is Neo-Noir or generic Low-Key Lighting: color neon rain, or a softly underexposed room with no hard edge. The tell is a filled shadow, dry pavement, and no slat texture on the wall.
Fix: kill the fill, add a venetian or tree cookie, wet the ground, and keep the palette silver.

sections.title: Questions

blocks.text: What is Film Noir in film?

A 1940s crime look built from hard, unfilled keys, gobo texture, wet streets, and eye-level 35mm or 50mm blocking. The picture withholds information. Silver contrast does the work that color would do in later noir.
Film Noir vs Neo-Noir

Film noir is low-key silver with tungsten practicals and wet-down bounce. Neo-noir keeps the guilty geometry but keys with color: sodium, neon, and contemporary flesh. If you can name a gel hue as the mood, you have left classic noir.
When should I use Film Noir?
When a crime scene needs the room to refuse the face: a doorway, a slatted office, a wet alley. Skip it for fashion-horror color, future screens, or any beat that needs a readable, filled close-up.
How do I prompt Film Noir for AI image or video?

Write: Film-noir treatment of [Subject], hard venetian gobos, unfilled far cheek, wet-down street, 50mm spherical, 1940s crime blocking. Specify the practical that motivates the key. Do not ask for color neon or a soft underexposed room.
